summary: How Christians know which books belong in the Bible, apostolic authority, recognized vs. authorized, the closing of the canon
readingInstruction: Read 2 Peter 1:16-21 and 2 Peter 3:15-16. Today is a doctrinal pause on the Bible itself: where it came from, why we have these sixty-six books, and why we trust them. Notice that Peter calls Paul’s letters Scripture.
settingTheScene: Christians believe the Bible is God’s word, but where did the list of books come from? Who decided which were included? Were they chosen by councils or simply recognized? These questions matter, especially for new believers who may hear that the Bible was assembled by powerful men centuries after Jesus. The answer is that the church recognized books that already carried God’s authority. Peter’s letter gives us early evidence of this process.
observation: “For we did not follow cleverly devised myths” (2 Peter 1:16).
“And we have something more sure, the prophetic word” (2 Peter 1:19).
“No prophecy of Scripture comes from someone’s own interpretation” (2 Peter 1:20).
“For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21).
“Our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him” (2 Peter 3:15).
“There are some things in them that are hard to understand” (2 Peter 3:16).
“Which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures” (2 Peter 3:16).
“And count the patience of our Lord as salvation” (2 Peter 3:15).
doctrinalFocus:
The Bible is a library of sixty-six books: thirty-nine in the Old Testament and twenty-seven in the New, written over about fifteen hundred years by some forty human authors. Yet it is one story, because it has one divine author. Peter says that “men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.” The human writers used their own personalities, styles, and research, and yet the product is God’s word. This is called inspiration. Because God is truthful, Scripture is also inerrant in what it affirms and sufficient for faith and life.

What is the canon? The word means “rule” or “standard.” The canon is the list of books recognized as the authoritative word of God. The church did not create the canon; it recognized it. Just as a person does not make a gold coin real by testing it, the church discerned which writings bore the marks of God’s voice.

The Old Testament canon. The Jewish community recognized the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings. Jesus and the apostles treated these as Scripture. Jesus spoke of “the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms” (Luke 24:44) and referred to the span from Abel to Zechariah (Luke 11:51), which covers the Hebrew Bible from first to last. The New Testament quotes nearly every book of the Old Testament as authoritative. The books called the Apocrypha or deuterocanonical books (Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, 1-2 Maccabees, and others) were written in the period between the testaments. The Roman Catholic Church formally included most of them at the Council of Trent in 1546, and Eastern Orthodox churches also include some. Protestants, following the Hebrew canon recognized by Jesus’ contemporaries, do not accept them as Scripture, though many find them useful for history. Those who hold to the Reformation view note that these books are never quoted as Scripture by Jesus or the apostles.

The New Testament canon. Early Christians recognized three features: apostolic origin (written by an apostle or someone connected to an apostle’s authority), conformity to the apostolic teaching, and widespread, continuous use in the churches. The four Gospels and Paul’s letters were widely accepted very early. Peter himself refers to Paul’s letters alongside “the other Scriptures” (2 Peter 3:16), showing that within the lifetime of the apostles, their writings were beginning to be received as Scripture. Lists from the second century (such as the Muratorian fragment) already resemble ours. Athanasius in AD 367 listed the twenty-seven books, and councils at Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) affirmed them. These councils confirmed what the churches already knew.

Why trust it? We believe the Bible is God’s word because of its own testimony, the witness of the Holy Spirit in believers, the character of Christ it reveals, its internal unity, and its historical reliability. And Jesus himself trusted the Scriptures: “Scripture cannot be broken” (John 10:35). If we trust Jesus, we trust the book he trusted. Because the apostles carry the authority he gave them, their writings complete the witness.

Peter also warns that Scripture can be twisted. Some of Paul’s letters are hard to understand, and the ignorant and unstable twist them. We should read with humility, compare Scripture with Scripture, and seek help from the church.
interpretation:
Peter’s first claim (1:16-18) is that the apostolic message is rooted in history. They did not follow clever myths. They were eyewitnesses. This is a concern about the truth of what happened, and it is the basis for the New Testament’s authority.

The second claim (1:19-21) is that the Old Testament prophets spoke by God. The verb “carried along” is the same used of a ship driven by the wind in Acts 27:15. The Spirit moved the authors, so that their words were truly theirs and truly God’s. The statement that no prophecy comes “from someone’s own interpretation” is best understood to mean that no prophet made up his message; the origin is God, not the prophet’s own insight. It also reminds us that interpretation matters: we should not twist Scripture to say what we want.

The third claim (3:15-16) is that Paul’s letters are among “the other Scriptures.” This is a remarkable thing for one apostle to say of another. It is also worth noting the humility of Peter: he admits some things in Paul are “hard to understand.” Even apostles had to wrestle with Scripture, which should encourage us when we find it hard.

Practically, this teaches us three things. First, we can trust the Bible because it comes from God. Second, we should study it carefully, because errors in interpretation have real consequences. Third, we should read it in the community of the church, where gifted teachers help us understand it.
connection: 2 Timothy 3:16-17 and Hebrews 1:1-2 speak of God’s word through prophets and his Son. Luke 24:25-27 and 24:44-47 show Jesus reading the Old Testament about himself. John 10:35 says Scripture cannot be broken. Matthew 5:17-18 affirms the Law and the Prophets. John 14:26 and 16:13 promise the Spirit’s help to the apostles. 1 Thessalonians 2:13 says the word is received as the word of God. 1 Timothy 5:18 quotes Luke as Scripture. Revelation 22:18-19 warns against adding to or taking away. Psalm 19:7-11 praises the word of the LORD. Acts 8:30-35 shows Philip explaining Scripture.
application:
Thank God today for the Bible and for the people who preserved and translated it.

If you have doubts about the Bible’s reliability, write down your questions and bring them to a pastor or a trusted friend. Many good books address them.

Read one passage this week that is “hard to understand,” and use a study Bible or commentary to help.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for giving you his word through the prophets and apostles.
Ask him to help you trust it as his word.
Ask him to give you a hunger for all of it.
